name: Kerr Black Hole in a Magnetic Universe
description: Kerr's rotating black hole inside Melvin's magnetic universe, the exact solution of the Einstein-Maxwell equations that Frederick Ernst and Walter Wild built in 1976 by a Harrison transformation of Kerr's metric. The hole carries the charge $Q = 2amB$ that Robert Wald found for a test field in 1974, and its ergoregion runs out to infinity in a tube beside the axis.
convention: The mass enters as the length $m = GM/c^2$, the spin parameter $a$ is a length, and the field strength $B$ is an inverse length. We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: Kerr's black hole, set in a magnetic field that runs along its axis of rotation, charges itself up [wald1974]. The calculation is Robert Wald's, from 1974, for a field too weak to bend spacetime, and it rests on a shortcut: in a vacuum spacetime a Killing vector "serves as a vector potential for a Maxwell test field", and Kerr's metric has two of them [wald1974]. Used as a potential, the Killing vector of the rotation is a magnetic field that is uniform far from the hole, and the Killing vector of the time translation is the field of a charge on the hole [wald1974, gibbons2013]. The spin drags the magnetic field round with it, the dragging induces an electric field, and a neutral hole lowers its energy by taking on charge [gibbons2013]. Wald's hole "will selectively accrete charges until its charge becomes" $Q = 2BJ$, with $B$ the strength of the field, $J$ the angular momentum of the hole, and $G = c = 1$ [wald1974].¶A magnetic field carries energy, and a uniform one left to its own gravity is Melvin's magnetic universe [melvin1964]. How does Kerr's hole fit inside it? The tool was B. Kent Harrison's transformation of 1968, which turns one solution of the Einstein-Maxwell equations with a Killing vector into another [harrison1968]. Applied to flat space it gives Melvin's universe, and applied to Schwarzschild's hole it gave Frederick Ernst a black hole in a magnetic universe in 1976 [ernst1976b, bicak2015]. With Walter Wild he ran Kerr and Newman's charged, spinning hole through it the same year, and they found the electromagnetic field for any charge [ernst1976c]. The whole metric they gave for "the particular case of charge" $Q = 2BJ$ with $J = ma$, which is Kerr's uncharged hole put through the transformation: the exact solution comes out carrying Wald's charge [ernst1976c, bicak2015, gibbons2013].¶No hole that spins or carries charge is static in Melvin's universe, a theorem of William Hiscock's from 1981 [hiscock1981b]. The axis has a conical singularity unless the angle $\phi$ is given a period longer than $2\pi$ [bicak2015]. The electric field measured on the axis stays constant far from the hole, so the spacetime does not approach Melvin's universe in every direction [hiscock1981b, bicak2015]. Gary Gibbons, A. H. Mujtaba, and Christopher Pope found the ergoregion of Ernst and Wild's hole running out to infinity in a tube beside the axis [gibbons2013]. In their words of 2013, "the dragging of inertial frames is so strong that even at infinity there is no Killing vector field which is everywhere timelike outside a compact set containing the black hole Killing horizon" [gibbons2013]. The ergoregion stays near the hole only for the charge $Q = jB(1 + \tfrac{1}{4}j^2B^4)$ with $j = am$, which in a weak field is half of Wald's [gibbons2013].¶Does the field thread the hole? For Wald's test field the flux through the upper half of the horizon is $\pi Br_+^2(1 - a^4/r_+^4)$, which falls as the hole spins up and vanishes at the limit $a = m$, where $r_+ = m$ [king1975, bicak1985, bicak2015]. By 1985 Jiří Bičák and V. Janiš had the general statement: an extreme Kerr hole shuts out every stationary test field that shares its axis, and the expulsion is called the Meissner effect of black holes, after the way a superconductor shuts out a magnetic field [bicak1985, bicak2000b, bicak2015]. Gibbons, Yi Pang, and Pope carried it to the exact solutions, where an extreme hole with no net charge keeps the field out as well [gibbons2014]. Close to its horizon every extreme magnetized hole has the geometry of an extreme Kerr-Newman hole, with $B$ absorbed into an effective spin and charge, a limit Bičák and Filip Hejda worked out in 2015 [bicak2015].¶A hole in Melvin's universe has no flat region far away, and the mass that is read off there for Kerr's hole is not defined for it [booth2015]. Its charge and angular momentum are integrals over any surface round the horizon, and for Ernst and Wild's hole they are $Q = 2amB$ and $J = am(1 - a^2m^2B^4)$ [booth2015]. The laws of black hole thermodynamics survive the field with one more term: Gibbons, Pang, and Pope wrote a first law with $-\mu\,dB$ in it and read $\mu$ as an induced magnetic moment [gibbons2014]. In 2016 M. Astorino, G. Compère, R. Oliveri, and N. Vandevoorde singled out the one mass that is integrable and equals Kerr and Newman's without the field, and it "coincides with the standard Christodoulou-Ruffini mass of a black hole as a function of the entropy, angular momentum and electric charge" [astorino2016].¶The gravity of the field matters only at distances of order $2/B$, the Melvin radius, and around a hole much smaller than that the test field is a good description [gibbons2013]. Magnetic field lines that thread a spinning hole can carry off its energy and angular momentum, the mechanism Roger Blandford and Roman Znajek proposed in 1977 as the engine of active galactic nuclei [blandford1977]. Ernst and Wild's metric is algebraically general, of Petrov type I [podolsky2025]. In 2025 Jiří Podolský and Hryhorii Ovcharenko found a second exact Kerr hole in a magnetic field, of type D, which is the Bertotti-Robinson universe when the mass is taken away [podolsky2025].

related.text: Switch the field off, $B = 0$, and Ernst and Wild's metric is Kerr's, with $m = GM/c^2$.
With the spin switched off, $a = 0$, it is Ernst's black hole in Melvin's universe, and with the mass switched off as well it is Melvin's universe itself [ernst1976b].
Kerr's hole with a charge of its own. Ernst and Wild put it through the same transformation, and their hole carries the charge $2amB$ even when the seed has none [ernst1976c, gibbons2013].
With no spin and no field, $a = 0$ and $B = 0$, it is Schwarzschild's black hole with $r_s = 2m$.
The other universe made of a uniform electromagnetic field. Podolský and Ovcharenko's Kerr hole of 2025 sits in a field that is Bertotti and Robinson's when its mass is taken away [podolsky2025].

Kerr's hole in the other uniform magnetic field, Bertotti and Robinson's, found by Jiří Podolský and Hryhorii Ovcharenko in 2025. It is of type D, its ergoregion stays near the hole, and it carries a charge close to $maB$ when $aB$ is small [podolsky2025, ovcharenko2026b].

coordinates.name: Ernst-Wild (Boyer-Lindquist)

parameters.description: Mass parameter of the Kerr seed, a length, $m = GM/c^2$
Spin parameter of the Kerr seed, a length; a horizon exists only for $a \le m$, and at $a = 0$ the metric is Ernst's black hole in Melvin's universe

Magnetic field strength of Melvin's universe around the hole, an inverse length, $B = \sqrt{G}\,B_0/c^2$ with $B_0$ the field in Gaussian units; at $B = 0$ the metric is Kerr's, and the vector potential is the one-form $\dfrac{c^2}{\sqrt{G}}\left(\dfrac{2}{B}\left(\omega - \dfrac{2mra}{A}\right)c\,dt + \dfrac{\partial_BH}{2H}\left(k\,d\phi - \omega\,c\,dt\right)\right)$
The value of $H$ on the axis; with it the axis is regular for $\phi$ of period $2\pi$
Kerr's $\Sigma$, which vanishes only on the ring $r = 0$, $\theta = \pi/2$
Kerr's $\Delta$, whose roots are the horizons
Kerr's $A$; the circle of $\phi$ in Kerr's metric has the squared radius $A\sin^2\theta/\Sigma$
Ernst and Wild's factor, which multiplies three terms of Kerr's line element and divides the fourth; it is 1 at $B = 0$ and Melvin's $\left(1 + B^2r^2\sin^2\theta/4\right)^2$ at $m = 0$ and $a = 0$

Dragging rate, an inverse length: an observer with no angular momentum circles at $d\phi/dt = c\,\omega/k$; at $B = 0$ it is Kerr's $2mra/A$, and on the horizon it is $\dfrac{a}{2mr_+} + \dfrac{amB^4\left(r_+ + m\right)}{2}$ at every $\theta$
The squared lapse of the slices of constant $t$, $H$ times Kerr's $\Delta\Sigma/A$
The factor on the plane of $r$ and $\theta$, $H$ times Kerr's $\Sigma$
The squared radius of the circle of $\phi$ over $k^2$, Kerr's $A\sin^2\theta/\Sigma$ divided by $H$

coordinates.convention: We use the coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ of Boyer and Lindquist's chart of the Kerr seed, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\phi$ the seed's angle divided by $k$, and write the line element in the functions $N$, $F$, $P$, and $\omega$ that the parameters define. The horizons are at $r_\pm = m \pm \sqrt{m^2 - a^2}$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Rotating Azimuth

parameters.description: Mass parameter of the Kerr seed, a length, $m = GM/c^2$
Spin parameter of the Kerr seed, a length; a horizon exists only for $a \le m$, and at $a = 0$ the metric is Ernst's black hole in Melvin's universe

Magnetic field strength of Melvin's universe around the hole, an inverse length, $B = \sqrt{G}\,B_0/c^2$ with $B_0$ the field in Gaussian units; at $B = 0$ the metric is Kerr's, and the vector potential is the one-form $\dfrac{c^2}{\sqrt{G}}\left(\dfrac{2}{B}\left(\omega - \dfrac{2mra}{A}\right)c\,dt + \dfrac{\partial_BH}{2H}\left(k\,d\phi - \omega\,c\,dt\right)\right)$
The value of $H$ on the axis; with it the axis is regular for $\phi$ of period $2\pi$
Kerr's $\Sigma$, which vanishes only on the ring $r = 0$, $\theta = \pi/2$
Kerr's $\Delta$, whose roots are the horizons
Kerr's $A$; the circle of $\phi$ in Kerr's metric has the squared radius $A\sin^2\theta/\Sigma$
Ernst and Wild's factor, which multiplies three terms of Kerr's line element and divides the fourth; it is 1 at $B = 0$ and Melvin's $\left(1 + B^2r^2\sin^2\theta/4\right)^2$ at $m = 0$ and $a = 0$

Dragging rate, an inverse length: an observer with no angular momentum circles at $d\phi/dt = c\,\omega/k$; at $B = 0$ it is Kerr's $2mra/A$, and on the horizon it is $\dfrac{a}{2mr_+} + \dfrac{amB^4\left(r_+ + m\right)}{2}$ at every $\theta$
The squared lapse of the slices of constant $t$, $H$ times Kerr's $\Delta\Sigma/A$
The factor on the plane of $r$ and $\theta$, $H$ times Kerr's $\Sigma$
The squared radius of the circle of $\phi$ over $k^2$, Kerr's $A\sin^2\theta/\Sigma$ divided by $H$
The rate at which the azimuth turns, an inverse length, $\tilde\phi = \phi - \Omega ct$; with $\Omega$ equal to $\omega/k$ on the horizon, $\partial_t$ is the null generator of the horizon

coordinates.convention: We use the coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \tilde\phi)$, with $\tilde\phi = \phi - \Omega ct$ an azimuth that turns at the constant rate $\Omega$ against Boyer and Lindquist's $\phi$, and write the line element in the functions $N$, $F$, $P$, and $\omega$ that the parameters define. The horizons are at $r_\pm = m \pm \sqrt{m^2 - a^2}$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
